To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

lung CoASH levels declined in Fischer-344 rats exposed to hyperoxic gas for 48 h, and this decline was not due to increases in lung GSSG levels, suggesting that CoASH is oxidized by oxidant stresses that do not increase GSSG levels in the lung.
hyperoxia decreases the lung contents of CoASH, CoASSG, and acetyl-CoA in Fischer-344 rats, but the CoASH/ CoASSG redox ratio is consistent with oxidant stresses on mitochondrial thiol status.
hyperoxia decreased lung tissue contents of CoA, CoASSG, and acetyl-CoA, but did not increase lung GSH/GSSC ratios.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the hypothesis that CoASH and CoA mixed disulfides are important biomarkers of intracellular oxidant stress and mitochondrial function in the lungs of rats exposed to hyperoxic conditions.
the role of intracellular thiol/disulfides, especially the mitochondrial CoASH/CoASG redox couple in the pathophysiology of lung injury.
the role of CoASH in lung mitochondrial function and the possible use of CoASH and CoASH/CoA mixed disulfides as biomarkers of oxidant stress in the lung.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
hyperoxia causes oxidant stress in the lungs of rats and that the CoASH/ CoASSG redox pair is a sensitive and useful indicator of this stress.
hyperoxia-induced decreases in the concentrations of CoASH in rat lungs are consistent with the hypothesis that intramitochondrial oxidant stresses may be generated during hyperoxia.

the decreases in lung tissue CoASH concentrations and the increases in lung GSSG contents observed in rats exposed to >95%, O2 for 24-48 h satisfy our criteria for an oxidatively stressed thiol/disulfid redox couple and that these changes may reflect oxidant stresses on the mitochondrial compartment of the lung.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the CoASH/ CoASSG thiol/disulf ide redox couple in the lung mitochondria is a sensitive indicator of oxidant stress, and that the CoASH levels per total lung tissue are decreased during hyperoxic lung injury, suggesting that the mitochondrial compartmentalization of CoASH is not maintained in these animals.

hyperoxic oxidant stresses in the lungs of rats are associated with decreases in lung CoASSG levels that are not accompanied by increases in CoASSG levels, suggesting that oxidant stresses are occurring preferentially on CoASSG, which is a more oxidized thiol than GSH.
the CoASH/ CoASSG redox state in lung tissues is a sensitive indicator of oxidant stresses, but the mechanisms responsible for the changes in the redox couple are not yet clear.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CoASH and CoASG are potential biomarkers for intramitochondrial oxidative stress in lung tissue.
the CoASH/ CoASSG redox status of the lungs in these animals was consistent with oxidant stress on the mitochondria.
the CoASH/ CoASSG redox couples in lung tissue and in mitochondria in particular are sensitive to hyperoxia and that these couples may be useful biomarkers of oxidant stresses in the mitochondria.
